summary_paragraph: A 50-year-old male with a history of psoriatic arthritis, insulin-dependent diabetes, morbid obesity, and recent MSSA cellulitis was admitted for bilateral neck swelling and facial edema causing shortness of breath. Initially admitted to the ICU for airway monitoring, he received IV dexamethasone and racemic epinephrine after developing respiratory distress during imaging. CT showed symmetrically enlarged parotid glands without abscess, consistent with sialadenitis. He was treated with IV clindamycin for possible bacterial superinfection, later discontinued as ENT and infectious disease concluded the inflammation was likely viral or related to his underlying psoriatic arthritis. A new pustular psoriasis rash on the chest and arms, triggered by steroid use, was managed with clobetasol. A fungal infection (tinea corporis) on the forearm was identified and treated with miconazole. His warfarin was held due to an INR of 4.8, then restarted and titrated to 4 mg daily with a therapeutic INR of 2.7 at discharge. He improved clinically, was weaned off IV therapy, and discharged home with outpatient follow-up and lab monitoring.
